system.name: Sirius
system.description: The brightest star in Earth's night sky, Sirius is a blue-white main-sequence star (A1V) located 8.6 light-years away. It has a faint white-dwarf companion, Sirius B, orbiting it every 50 years.

siriusa.name: Sirius A
siriusa.description: An A1V blue-white main-sequence star about twice the Sun's mass and 1.7 times its diameter, making it the most luminous star in Earth's night sky at just 8.6 light-years away. Its name derives from the ancient Greek word for 'glowing' or 'scorching'.
siriusa.funFact: Ancient Egyptians tracked the annual first rising of Sirius at dawn to predict the Nile flood — the event was so important that they built their calendar around it, marking the beginning of the year.

siriusb.name: Sirius B
siriusb.description: A DA2 white dwarf — the remnant core of a star that once outshone Sirius A. Despite being barely larger than Earth, Sirius B packs nearly the full mass of our Sun, giving it an extraordinary density. It was predicted to exist before being directly observed, a triumph of 19th-century astronomy.
siriusb.funFact: Sirius B was detected by its gravitational pull on Sirius A before it was ever seen directly — making it one of the first objects discovered through its influence on another star rather than its own light.
